title: When "Make It Run" Becomes a Security Incident
excerpt: How a university platform went from a successful prototype to a serious privacy and security failure—and how it should be rebuilt using secure design principles.
content:
From Prototype to Production

The university platform in this case shows a problem in modern software development: a system can be technically functional while being fundamentally unsafe. Three students made a mobile-and-web platform in less than 72 hours with a lot of help from an AI coding assistant. The prototype worked enough to win a hackathon prize and organizations soon started using it for real tasks. The problem was that the developers treated a prototype as if it were ready for production.

The platform eventually held sensitive information, including student numbers, phone numbers, identification photos, GCash payment references, and private group messages. However, the security measures stayed at the level of a show. A user could change a profile number in a URL and see another student's information. Database passwords and an API key were put into a GitHub repository. Accounts had too much access to the database, error messages showed too much detail, and the system used plain HTTP.

These issues were not individual coding errors. They showed violations of Secure Design Principles. The important takeaway is that security has to be built into a system before it is responsible for protecting real people's information.

Horizon One: The First Hours and Days

The first thing would be to stop the problem. I would take the application offline and put it into maintenance mode. Since the application is sharing information, leaving it online while checking it would make things worse. This goes back to the principle of safe defaults because access would default to being blocked rather than allowing people who should not have access to see records.

Next, I would replace every password and key that was found in the public GitHub repository. The exposed database password and payment API key should be thought of as broken even if there is no proof that someone used them. A secret that is out in the open cannot be trusted anymore. New passwords and keys should be kept in environment variables or a special secrets-management system instead of in the code. This follows least privilege and economy of mechanism by making sure only the right people and parts of the system can access important secrets.

I would also look into what information might have been seen. The team should check application logs, database access logs, GitHub history, and any other records to find out how much and how long the information was exposed. This is important because just removing the problem from the system does not tell us if someone already saw the data.

The broken profile authorization is very serious. The application used a profile identifier from the URL without checking if the logged-in user was allowed to see that record. This violates complete mediation, which means every time someone tries to see something, the system has to check if they are allowed. Just being logged in is not enough. The system must also check if the logged-in user is allowed to perform the action on that record.

For example, asking for /profile/1049 should not automatically give profile 1049. The server has to check the user's identity and permission before giving the record. Authorization checks must happen on the server and not rely on hidden parts of the interface or random URLs.

The database permissions should also be checked right away. Giving every account access to the database goes against least privilege. Users and parts of the system should only get the permissions they need for their job. If one account is compromised, it should not automatically give access to all the data of hundreds of students.

Finally, detailed error messages should be turned off in production. Error messages should be clear enough for people to know something is wrong without showing database queries, file paths, passwords, framework details, or anything else that could be used by someone trying to cause harm. This supports defense in depth because even if another problem exists, error handling does not give an attacker additional information.

Horizon Two: Rebuilding the System Properly

After the urgent problem is fixed, I would rebuild the application with security being the focus, not just fixing the individual issues.

The first big change would be a proper system for authentication and authorization. Every sensitive request would go through server-side checks for permission. This brings back complete mediation. The application should use a deny-by-default model where access is given only when it is allowed.

I would also use least privilege throughout the system. Database accounts should have limited access. A part of the system that reads membership information should not also have permission to delete payment records. Admin functions should need permission, and users should only see the things that belong to their group or account.

The system should also use defense in depth. Security should not depend on one thing. HTTPS should protect the way clients and servers communicate. Authentication should protect accounts. Authorization should protect the things users want to see. Database access should keep damage low if the app is broken. Input checks should stop unexpected data. Logging and monitoring should help find unusual behavior. All these parts together give multiple layers of protection.

The principle of separation of privilege is also important. Sensitive actions should need extra permission and should not just be available to anyone who is logged in. For example, changing who owns an organization, seeing financial information, or handling admin accounts could require higher access.

The developers should also use open design. Security should not be based on hiding URLs or assuming attackers will not find the app's structure. The case relied on people not knowing the structure of the URLs. That is not a good way to be secure. A secure app should still be safe even if people know its parts and how it works.

The app should also follow psychological acceptability. Security should be easy for users to understand and use. If security steps are confusing, users might try to get around them. Good defaults, messages about who can see what, and simple account management features make it easier for users to be safe.

The way the team develops the app should change too. Before adding features, the team should think about what could go wrong. Code reviews should specifically look at authentication, authorization, secrets, input checks, error handling, and data leaks. Automated security tests should also be part of the development process.

The Role of AI Coding Assistants

AI coding assistants can make building apps faster, but speed can give a false sense of safety: code that works is not always safe.

In this case, the AI-generated code made the app work. It probably made database access easier, but there were not enough checks for who could do what and there were unsafe ways to show errors. These are choices that might be acceptable for a quick test but are not okay for software that holds real student data.

The blame still lies with the developers. AI should be a helper, not a security expert. Developers must check the code that AI writes, understand what it does, test it, and make sure it follows security rules.

A good rule is that developers should not only ask, "Does this code work?" They should also ask, "Who can see this?", "What happens if this account is compromised?", "What information does this error share?", and "What happens if someone changes this ID?"

AI can make code, but it cannot take responsibility for what the code does.

RA No. 10173 and Privacy Responsibilities

This situation is also linked to the Philippines Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The app was handling details like names, student numbers, phone numbers, photos, payment references, and private messages.

Developers working on apps that handle information cannot see security as just a technical thing. Their choices affect whether personal data is kept safe. They need rules, physical steps, and technical ways to protect personal data from people who should not see it, share it, change it, or do anything else with it.

This case shows why privacy should be considered when making a system, not after it is built. If developers know their app will hold documents and financial information, those risks should shape how the app is built from the start.

Privacy is not only the job of a privacy officer or someone in charge. Developers decide what data is collected, where it is kept, who can see it, how users log in, and what happens if something goes wrong. Those choices directly affect how safe people's data is.

Speed vs. Responsibility

The students' biggest mistake was not using AI, working fast, or building a prototype. The real mistake was letting a test version become a real system without changing the way security was handled.

Fast building is useful in competitions and early tests. When a system starts holding real people's data, the standards have to change. The main goal becomes keeping the people who trust the system safe.

Principles like least privilege, complete mediation, safe defaults, defense in depth, separation of privilege, open design, economy of mechanism, and psychological acceptability help make that change.

AI tools help make apps faster. That makes secure development more important, not less. Developers must understand that code that looks good can still have security issues.

The goal is not to choose between making things fast or making them safe. The goal is to recognize when a project moves from being an experiment to something people depend on, and make sure that security, privacy, and responsibility grow with it. When an app has data from hundreds of students, "make it work" is no longer enough. The app must also be built so it deserves the trust those students placed in it.
